passage: I'm Pankaj, Elizabeth's younger brother, so I saw the whole thing from the sofa. Mummy said no to the class trip to the hill station. Elizabeth shouted, "You never trust me!" and slammed her bedroom door so hard the calendar fell off the wall. Twenty minutes later she came out, eyes red, and sat at the dining table with a notebook. "Mummy, I really want to go. Everyone in my group is going, and I've never been anywhere without you. I know you're scared because of the ghat roads. What if I call you every night at nine, give you the teacher's number and share a room with Riya?" Mummy was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "Let me speak to your teacher tomorrow." I don't know if Elizabeth was calm inside, but she sounded calm.

qa.q: What fell off the wall when Elizabeth slammed the door?
qa.a: The calendar fell off the wall.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she shouted "You never trust me!"?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt controlled and angry at the refusal, which is why she shouted and slammed the door.

qa.q: What made Elizabeth's second try work better?
qa.a: She stated her need, named Mummy's fear about the ghat roads and offered conditions, like nightly calls and the teacher's number, instead of shouting.

qa.q: How might Mummy see Elizabeth's notebook proposal?
qa.a: Mummy probably feels her fear was heard and trusts Elizabeth more, which is why she agrees to speak to the teacher.

grounding: Illustrates a teen who argues and slams a door over a parent's restriction, then states the need, acknowledges the fear and proposes conditions.

passage:
Monday: His mother, Lakshmi, announced that Akash's phone would stay in the kitchen after ten. "You're controlling my whole life!" he shouted, and banged his cupboard shut.
Wednesday: Late at night Akash noticed Amma sitting up with his exam timetable, rubbing her eyes. He remembered she had caught him scrolling at 2 a.m. twice last week. He knocked on her door. "I get that you're worried about my sleep. But I need the phone for the group study call till ten-thirty on weeknights."
Saturday: They sat down and agreed: phone in the kitchen by ten-thirty on school nights, eleven on weekends, and a review after exams if his marks held up. Akash still grumbled, but he put the phone on the kitchen shelf himself.

qa.q: When did Amma first want Akash's phone in the kitchen?
qa.a: Amma wanted it in the kitchen after ten.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling on Monday when he banged the cupboard?
qa.a: Akash felt controlled and angry, as if Amma was running his whole life.

qa.q: Which step turned the argument into an agreement?
qa.a: Akash named Amma's worry about his sleep and proposed specific conditions, like ten-thirty on school nights and a review after exams.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi see Akash knocking on her door on Wednesday?
qa.a: Lakshmi likely feels relieved that he understood her worry and is talking instead of shouting.

grounding: Shows a teen moving over several days from shouting about a phone limit to naming his mother's worry and negotiating conditions.

passage:
Friday: Siddharth told Papa he was at Kunal's house studying. Really they were at the gaming café across town until nine. It felt easy.
Sunday: Papa ran into Kunal's mother at the market. "Kunal was out all Friday," she said. That night Papa didn't shout. He just said, "I'd rather hear a hard truth than a smooth lie," and asked Siddharth to share his location for a month. Siddharth's face burned.
The next Friday: Siddharth tried something new. "Papa, I want to go to the gaming café with Kunal. It's a safe place, I'll be back by eight-thirty, and you can call me there." Papa looked at him for a long moment. "Eight-thirty. And thank you for asking."

qa.q: Where were Siddharth and Kunal really on Friday?
qa.a: They were at the gaming café across town until nine.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when his face burned on Sunday?
qa.a: Siddharth felt ashamed and guilty at being caught, seeing that Papa's trust had been damaged.

qa.q: What changed the next Friday, and why did it work?
qa.a: Siddharth asked honestly, with a safe plan and a return time, so Papa could say yes without being deceived.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt after hearing from Kunal's mother?
qa.a: Papa probably felt hurt and worried, since he had believed Siddharth was studying safely at Kunal's.

grounding: Illustrates a teen whose lie about where he was costs trust, and who then tries honest negotiation instead.

passage: Imran, you think I don't know why your Ammi is upset? Sit. Your Pradeep Uncle once did the same. At fifteen I told my mother I was at a friend's house for a science project. Really, I took the bus to Nashik for a cricket match. The bus broke down on the way back, and I got home at midnight. My mother was on the doorstep with the neighbours; she had called every friend I had. The worst part wasn't the scolding. For a year after that, every time I said "I'm at the library," she checked. One lie cost me a whole year of being believed. Next time, tell Ammi what you want to do, and make a plan she can say yes to.

qa.q: Where did Pradeep Uncle really go at fifteen?
qa.a: He took the bus to Nashik for a cricket match.

qa.q: What might Pradeep have felt on seeing his mother on the doorstep with the neighbours?
qa.a: Pradeep probably felt ashamed and frightened, seeing how worried she had been.

qa.q: Which choice in the story did the lasting damage, and what would have been better?
qa.a: The lie about the science project cost a year of trust; asking honestly with a plan and a return time could have avoided it.

qa.q: How did Pradeep's mother see his "I'm at the library" in the year after?
qa.a: She could no longer take his word, so she felt anxious and checked every time.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, how a teen's lie about his whereabouts brought short freedom and a long loss of trust.

passage:
Mum: You've been in your room since Friday. Dinner's ready 🙂
Mum: Urmila?
Mum: I know you're upset about Ira's sleepover.
Urmila: im fine
Mum: You haven't spoken at dinner for three days. That doesn't look fine.
Urmila: whatever
Mum: I won't force you. But I can't help with something I don't know about.
(twenty minutes later)
Urmila: ok. I feel left out and kind of embarrassed. everyone in the group chat is posting outfits and I have to say my mum said no
Mum: Thank you for telling me. That sounds really hard 😔
Mum: The overnight is still a no. But could you go till 9 and I pick you up?
Urmila: ...maybe. can we talk at dinner
Mum: Yes. Paneer's on the table.

qa.q: How long had Urmila been silent at dinner?
qa.a: Urmila hadn't spoken at dinner for three days.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when she finally texted?
qa.a: Urmila felt left out and embarrassed that everyone else was going to Ira's sleepover.

qa.q: What finally opened the door to help?
qa.a: Naming the feeling in one message let Mum understand and offer a middle option, going till 9 with a pickup.

qa.q: How might Mum have felt during the three silent days?
qa.a: Mum likely felt worried and shut out, unable to help without knowing what was wrong.

grounding: Illustrates a teen withdrawing into silence after a parent's no, and how naming the feeling in a sentence lets help in.

passage: Since Papa said she couldn't cycle to the evening maths class in the next village any more, Nikita had stopped talking. She ate quickly, went to the back room and kept the door shut, even when the neighbours came for tea. Her cousin Devika, visiting from Indore for the holidays, found her staring at the ceiling fan. "You're allowed to be angry, you know. But nobody can help a wall." Nikita was quiet for a long time. Then: "I'm scared I'll fail maths without that class. And I'm angry he didn't even ask me." Devika squeezed her hand. "Say exactly that to him." That night, Nikita did. Papa rubbed his forehead. "The road has no lights, beti. But maybe the Sharma girls' father can drive you both. I'll ask him tomorrow."

qa.q: Where was Nikita's evening maths class?
qa.a: It was in the next village.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling behind her silence?
qa.a: Nikita felt scared of failing maths and angry that Papa hadn't asked her, so she shut herself in the back room.

qa.q: What helped Nikita break the silence?
qa.a: Devika's gentle nudge helped Nikita put the fear and anger into one clear sentence and say it to Papa.

qa.q: How does Papa see the problem once Nikita speaks?
qa.a: Papa sees that his worry was the unlit road, not holding her back, and starts looking for a safe way for her to attend.

grounding: Shows a teen shutting herself away after a parent's restriction, and how one honest sentence about her feelings opens a solution.

passage:
At thirteen: Afreen begged to walk home alone from tuition like Gautam and the others. Ammi said no and waited at the gate every evening in her old dupatta. Afreen walked three steps ahead, mortified.
At fifteen: Ammi finally agreed, after Afreen had learned every shortcut, the shopkeepers' names and which lanes flooded. Afreen rolled her eyes at the rules but kept them.
At seventeen: Afreen's little cousin started tuition and cried to walk alone. Afreen heard herself say, "Not yet. I'll come." Waiting at that same gate, she suddenly understood those two years of Ammi standing there in the heat. That evening she bought Ammi's favourite kulfi on the way home and didn't say why.

qa.q: What did Afreen buy for Ammi on the way home at seventeen?
qa.a: Afreen bought Ammi's favourite kulfi.

qa.q: What did Afreen feel while waiting at the gate at seventeen?
qa.a: Afreen felt a rush of understanding and grateful love for Ammi, seeing that Ammi's waiting had been care, not control.

qa.q: What could help a teen like Afreen at thirteen feel less mortified?
qa.a: If Ammi explained that walking alone would come once the routes were learned, Afreen could see the limit as temporary care.

qa.q: How might Ammi experience the kulfi with no explanation?
qa.a: Ammi might feel quietly touched, sensing something had shifted in Afreen even without words 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a teen realising, years after a parent's strict limit, that it was care, as she grows old enough to see the love behind it.

passage: Pradeep, you're sulking because your father won't let you ride the scooter before your licence. Let your Harsha Mama tell you something. At sixteen I was furious with my own father over the same rule. My friends rode their elder brothers' bikes to school and laughed at me pedalling behind them. I called him old-fashioned and didn't speak to him for a week. The year after, one of those friends skidded on wet gravel and was in plaster for months. Even then I didn't thank my father. It took until my own son turned fifteen and I heard myself saying, "Not until you're trained." That rule wasn't about control. It was him being scared for me, and loving me too much to say yes.

qa.q: What happened to one of the friends who rode bikes?
qa.a: One of those friends skidded on wet gravel and was in plaster for months.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling at sixteen about the father's rule?
qa.a: Harsha felt furious and embarrassed, pedalling behind friends who laughed, and called the father old-fashioned.

qa.q: Which moment in the story brought the real understanding, and why?
qa.a: Hearing himself tell his own son "Not until you're trained" showed Harsha that the rule came from fear and love, not control.

qa.q: How might Harsha's father have felt during that week of silence?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and lonely but held firm because he was scared for his son's safety.

grounding: Shows, in an uncle's memory, a teen resenting a parent's limit and only years later seeing the love behind it.

passage: Zeenat, I saw you check that boy's page four times during dinner, so let your Parveen Khala tell you a story. When I was sixteen, there was Adil, who sang at every college function. I decided he was perfect: kind, deep, the best singer alive. I refreshed his page on the cyber café computer so often the owner started charging me extra. My friend Shabnam finally said, "You've never talked to him. Just watch how he treats people." So I watched. He mocked the canteen boy for spilling tea, and he talked over everyone at practice. Nothing like the Adil in my head. The crush melted in a week. I'm not saying your boy is like that. Just look at what he does, not what you imagine.

qa.q: Where did Parveen refresh Adil's page?
qa.a: Parveen refreshed his page on the cyber café computer.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling about Adil before the reality check?
qa.a: Parveen felt infatuated and excited, imagining Adil as perfect though they had never talked.

qa.q: Which choice in the story broke the spell, and why?
qa.a: Following Shabnam's advice to watch Adil's real behaviour showed how he treated the canteen boy, which the ideal picture had hidden.

qa.q: How might the canteen boy have felt when Adil mocked him?
qa.a: The canteen boy probably felt humiliated and small over a simple spill.

grounding: Illustrates a teen idealising a crush and checking his page constantly, until a friend's advice and his real behaviour bring a reality check.

passage: It was the week of board pre-exams, and Kalyani's phone battery kept dying because she checked Rohan's profile every few minutes: a new photo with his guitar, a song lyric, a sunset. In her head he was gentle and brilliant. Arohi grabbed the phone during a study break in the library. "You've refreshed this eleven times in an hour. What do you actually know about him?" Kalyani opened her mouth and found nothing. Arohi went on, softer. "In our physics group he never did his part, and he laughed when Meera stammered." Kalyani remembered that laugh; she had pretended not to hear it. That evening she muted his posts until exams ended. It stung, but her chemistry notes finally made sense.

qa.q: How many times had Kalyani refreshed the profile in an hour?
qa.a: Kalyani had refreshed it eleven times in an hour.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she opened her mouth and found nothing?
qa.a: Kalyani felt caught out and a little embarrassed, realising she knew almost nothing real about Rohan.

qa.q: What small step helped Kalyani during exam week?
qa.a: Muting Rohan's posts until exams ended cut the constant checking and let her focus on chemistry.

qa.q: How does Arohi see Kalyani's constant checking?
qa.a: Arohi seems worried for her friend and a bit frustrated, so she offers an honest reality check about Rohan's behaviour.

grounding: Shows a teen idealising a crush during exam week, and a friend's honesty plus remembered behaviour bringing her back to reality.

passage: On the last day of the school term in Osaka, Yuki finally gave Sofia the note he had rewritten six times: would she go to the summer festival with him? Sofia read it by the shoe lockers, bit her lip and said gently, "You're really nice, Yuki. But I only like you as a friend. I'm sorry." Yuki said, "It's fine!" too loudly and walked home the long way, cheeks burning. For three days he didn't answer the class chat. He felt like everyone knew. On the fourth day his older cousin Kenji dragged him to the batting cages. "She said no to a festival, not to you," Kenji said between swings. By the end of the week, Yuki had gone to the festival anyway, with Kenji and two friends, and laughed more than he expected.

qa.q: Where did Sofia read Yuki's note?
qa.a: Sofia read it by the shoe lockers.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling as he walked home the long way?
qa.a: Yuki felt shattered and embarrassed, sure that everyone knew about the rejection.

qa.q: What helped Yuki begin to heal?
qa.a: Time, his cousin Kenji's company at the batting cages and the reminder that the no was about a festival, not his worth, helped him go out again.

qa.q: How might Sofia have felt saying no by the lockers?
qa.a: Sofia probably felt awkward and sorry, trying to be gentle because she liked Yuki as a friend.

grounding: Illustrates a teen feeling crushed and embarrassed after a gentle no, and healing through time, support and remembering it is not a verdict on his worth.

passage: In the school sick room, Binita lay on the cot pretending to have a headache. An hour earlier, at the science club, she had asked Sarita's brother Rohit, in Class 12, if he'd like to walk to the book fair with her. He'd laughed, not unkindly. "You're Sarita's little friend! No, sorry." Two boys nearby had grinned. Binita wanted the floor to swallow her. Sister Mary, the school nurse, sat on the stool beside her. "Headaches don't usually come with red eyes. Want to tell me?" Binita blurted it out. Sister Mary nodded. "That stings. But one no from one person isn't a mark on who you are." Later Sarita came in with a samosa. "My brother is an idiot about feelings. You're brave." Binita laughed, and the ache eased a little.

qa.q: Where was Binita lying when Sister Mary came in?
qa.a: Binita lay on the cot in the school sick room.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling after Rohit laughed and said no?
qa.a: Binita felt embarrassed and crushed, wishing the floor would swallow her, especially with the boys grinning.

qa.q: How did Sister Mary support Binita?
qa.a: Sister Mary noticed the red eyes, invited Binita to talk and reminded her that one no from one person isn't a mark on who she is.

qa.q: How might Sarita see Binita asking her brother out?
qa.a: Sarita seems to see it as brave rather than foolish, and cares enough to bring a samosa and cheer Binita up.

grounding: Shows a teen feeling shattered and embarrassed after a rejection, and support from an adult and a friend reminding her it is not a verdict on her worth.

passage: Afreen, you said your boyfriend checks your messages because he loves you. Let your Phuphi Rubina tell you about a boy I knew. I was sixteen. Chinmay called me every hour to ask where I was. He said my friends were a bad influence, so I stopped going to Salma's house. If I laughed with a boy in class, he went silent for a day and said, "I guess I'm not enough for you." I felt guilty all the time, and I told myself this was love. One evening my elder sister read over my shoulder and asked, "Do you feel free, or watched?" I cried, because I knew. She sat with me while I told Abba, and I ended it that week. Love gives you room, beta. Control takes it away.

qa.q: How often did Chinmay call Rubina?
qa.a: Chinmay called every hour to ask where Rubina was.

qa.q: What was Rubina feeling during the relationship with Chinmay?
qa.a: Rubina felt guilty all the time and confused, mistaking Chinmay's jealousy and checking for love.

qa.q: Which moment in the story helped Rubina see the control, and why?
qa.a: The sister's question, "Do you feel free, or watched?", helped Rubina name the checking, the isolation and the guilt-tripping, then tell Abba and end it.

qa.q: How might Salma have experienced Rubina no longer coming over?
qa.a: Salma probably felt confused and hurt, losing a friend without knowing that Chinmay was pushing Rubina away.

grounding: Illustrates, through an aunt's memory, a teen mistaking jealousy and monitoring for love and learning to spot control, isolation and guilt-tripping.

passage: The storm had knocked out the power in Jomon's part of Kottayam, his phone was at three per cent, and Farida hadn't replied for an hour. He typed fast. "Where are you? Who's there? Send a photo." Then: "If you really cared, you'd answer me." Twenty messages before the screen died. He told himself it was because he loved her. The next morning the school counsellor ran a session on relationships and wrote a list on the board: checking where someone is all the time, cutting them off from friends, guilt-tripping. Jomon went cold. That was his list. At lunch he found Farida. "Those messages last night. That wasn't love, that was me trying to control you. I'm sorry. I'll stop asking for photos." Farida nodded slowly. "I was at my cousin's. My phone was charging."

qa.q: What list did the counsellor write on the board?
qa.a: Checking where someone is all the time, cutting them off from friends, and guilt-tripping.

qa.q: Why did Jomon go cold during the counsellor's session?
qa.a: Jomon felt shocked and ashamed, recognising his own messages in the list of controlling behaviour.

qa.q: What did Jomon do after recognising the warning signs?
qa.a: He named his messages as control, apologised to Farida and promised to stop asking for photos.

qa.q: How might Farida have felt seeing twenty messages when her phone came back on?
qa.a: Farida likely felt pressured and uneasy, even guilty, though she had only been charging her phone at her cousin's.

grounding: Shows a teen who confused jealous monitoring with love recognising control and guilt-tripping as warning signs in his own messages.

passage:
Monday: Walking out of the school gate, Kamal glanced at Lavanya's hand. "Can I?" She smiled but shook her head. "Not in front of everyone yet." "Okay," he said, and meant it.
Thursday: Lavanya had district football trials on Saturday and had to skip their evening walks all week. Kamal texted, "Go get it ⚽ Tell me how practice went." He didn't sulk once.
Saturday: After she made the squad, Lavanya admitted something. "I'm not ready for the movie with just us. Is that weird?" Kamal shrugged. "Not weird. Let's go with Riya and Tom, then." Lavanya let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding.

qa.q: What were Lavanya's trials for?
qa.a: Lavanya had district football trials on Saturday.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when she admitted she wasn't ready for the movie?
qa.a: Lavanya felt nervous about saying it, then relieved when Kamal accepted it without fuss.

qa.q: Which of Kamal's choices showed respectful care?
qa.a: Asking before holding hands, accepting "not yet", backing her trials and suggesting going with friends all showed consent, space and support.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel skipping their evening walks all week?
qa.a: Kamal may miss her, but feels proud of her and chooses support over sulking.

grounding: Illustrates a teen relationship where care includes asking consent, giving space, honesty and backing the partner's goals.

passage: Suraj, you asked how I knew Shabana was the one. Your old Yusuf Chacha will tell you, but it isn't about fireworks. We were seventeen, in the same tuition class in Bhopal. I liked her so much my ears went red. The first time I walked her home, I asked, "May I walk with you tomorrow too?" She said, "Only on Tuesdays. Other days I study with my cousins." So it was only Tuesdays. When she said she wanted to become a teacher before anyone talked of marriage, I carried her books to the college entrance exam and waited outside for three hours. And when I failed my own exam, I told her the truth instead of pretending. She said that was when she began to trust me.

qa.q: Which day did Shabana agree to be walked home?
qa.a: Shabana agreed only on Tuesdays.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when his ears went red in tuition class?
qa.a: Yusuf felt shy and strongly drawn to Shabana, liking her so much he blushed.

qa.q: Which choice in the story built Shabana's trust, and why?
qa.a: Telling her the truth about failing his exam instead of pretending showed honesty, which she said was when she began to trust him.

qa.q: How might Shabana have seen Yusuf waiting three hours outside her exam?
qa.a: Shabana probably felt supported and respected, since he backed her goal of becoming a teacher.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, teenage affection built on asking, respecting limits, honesty and supporting the other person's goals.

passage: By second period, half of Class 10 in their Kolkata school knew that Minakshi's parents were separating. She had told only one person: Alka. Minakshi's hands shook as she typed in the class group: "Want to know Alka's secret? She copied her whole science project from her cousin." Her thumb hovered over send. She hated Alka right then. She wanted her to feel exactly this. Instead she deleted it, walked twice around the basketball court, and sat on the steps until her breathing slowed. After school she caught Alka alone near the cycle stand. "I told you that because I trusted you. Why?" Alka's face crumpled. "I told Nisha, and she told everyone. I'm so sorry." Minakshi didn't forgive her yet. "I need time to decide if I can trust you again."

qa.q: Who had Minakshi told about her parents?
qa.a: Minakshi had told only one person: Alka.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling as her thumb hovered over send?
qa.a: Minakshi felt betrayed and full of hatred, wanting Alka to feel the same exposure.

qa.q: Which steps made Minakshi's path wiser than exposing Alka?
qa.a: She deleted the post, walked to cool down, confronted Alka privately and took time to decide about trust.

qa.q: How does Alka see Minakshi's question at the cycle stand?
qa.a: Alka feels ashamed and sorry, knowing her slip to Nisha hurt her best friend badly.

grounding: Illustrates a teen betrayed by a best friend who wants to expose her back, but cools down, confronts her privately and takes time to decide about trust.

passage:
"You told Arjun I still see a speech therapist?"
"Vaibhav, wait—"
"Now the whole cricket team's doing the voice. You know what I could tell them about you? About your dad's shop?"
"..."
"I'm not going to. I thought about it all through maths. I wanted to. But that's not me."
"I'm sorry. Arjun asked why you leave early on Thursdays and I just... said it. I didn't think."
"You didn't think, and now I hear the voice every practice."
"I'll tell Arjun it's not funny. I'll tell the whole team."
"Do that first. Then we'll see."
"Are we still friends?"
"I don't know yet, Noor. Ask me next week."

qa.q: Who did Noor tell about the speech therapist?
qa.a: Noor told Arjun.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling all through maths?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt betrayed and angry, and was tempted to expose Noor back by telling the team about the dad's shop.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do instead of exposing Noor, and why was it wiser?
qa.a: He confronted Noor privately, asked for the harm to be fixed first and gave himself a week to decide about trust, so he didn't add more hurt.

qa.q: How might Noor feel hearing "Ask me next week"?
qa.a: Noor probably feels anxious and ashamed, but also has a clear chance to rebuild trust by fixing things with the team.

grounding: Shows a teen furious at a best friend's betrayal choosing a private confrontation over revenge and waiting to decide about trust.

passage: Lavanya, you asked if you should forgive Sneha. Your Uma Athai has a story. When I was fifteen, my best friend Kamala told the whole hostel that I was scared of the dark and slept with a torch. They laughed for weeks. Kamala came to me on a Sunday, crying, with a letter she had written. She didn't say "sorry if you felt bad." She said, "I did it to look funny. It was cruel." She told the girls herself, the same day. I forgave her. But after that, I didn't tell her the things I kept for my diary. We've been friends for forty years, and she still brings me a torch every Diwali as a joke. Forgiving her didn't mean forgetting. It meant choosing her, carefully.

qa.q: What did Kamala tell the whole hostel?
qa.a: Kamala told the hostel that Uma was scared of the dark and slept with a torch.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when the hostel laughed for weeks?
qa.a: Uma felt betrayed and humiliated that her best friend had shared something private.

qa.q: Which part of Kamala's apology made forgiveness possible?
qa.a: Kamala named exactly what she did and why, without excuses, and told the girls herself the same day.

qa.q: How might Kamala feel bringing a torch every Diwali?
qa.a: Kamala probably feels grateful to be forgiven, and the joke shows she remembers the hurt instead of hiding from it.

grounding: Illustrates, in an aunt's memory, a teen forgiving a best friend after a sincere apology while sharing less, since forgiving is not forgetting.

passage: With two days left to finish their group project on water harvesting, Kavitha had to sit next to Gautam in the crowded school library. A week earlier he had told her cousin that she'd secretly applied to an art college in Baroda, and the news reached her parents before she could tell them herself. Now he slid a note across the table: "I told because I was showing off that I knew. It wasn't mine to tell. I'm really sorry, and I'll say so to your parents if it helps." Kavitha read it twice. The apology named exactly what he had done. She wrote back: "I forgive you. But I'm keeping some things to myself for a while." He nodded. They finished the rainfall chart by closing time.

qa.q: What was the group project about?
qa.a: The group project was on water harvesting.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling as she read Gautam's note twice?
qa.a: Kavitha still felt hurt by the betrayal, but the specific, honest apology softened her enough to forgive.

qa.q: How did Kavitha balance forgiveness with caution?
qa.a: She forgave Gautam but decided to keep some things to herself for a while, since forgiving is not forgetting.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel reading "I'm keeping some things to myself"?
qa.a: Gautam may feel relieved to be forgiven yet also stung, understanding he has to earn back her full trust.

grounding: Shows a teen forgiving a friend's betrayal after a sincere apology while choosing to share less for now.
